source_text: Certainly an Englishman, it was more doubtful whether Phileas Fogg was a Londoner. He was never seen on ’Change, nor at the Bank, nor in the counting-rooms of the “City”; no ships ever came into London docks of which he was the owner; he had no public employment; he had never been entered at any of the Inns of Court, either at the Temple, or Lincoln’s Inn, or Gray’s Inn; nor had his voice ever resounded in the Court of Chancery, or in the Exchequer, or the Queen’s Bench, or the Ecclesiastical Courts. He certainly was not a manufacturer; nor was he a merchant or a gentleman farmer. His name was strange to the scientific and learned societies, and he never was known to take part in the sage deliberations of the Royal Institution or the London Institution, the Artisan’s Association, or the Institution of Arts and Sciences. He belonged, in fact, to none of the numerous societies which swarm in the English capital, from the Harmonic to that of the Entomologists, founded mainly for the purpose of abolishing pernicious insects.
modern_text: An Englishman, certainly. Whether he was a Londoner was less clear. He was never seen on ’Change, nor at the Bank, nor in the counting-rooms of the “City”; no ships ever came into London docks of which he was the owner; he held no public office; he had never been entered at any of the Inns of Court—not the Temple, not Lincoln’s Inn, not Gray’s Inn—nor had his voice ever sounded in the Court of Chancery, or the Exchequer, or the Queen’s Bench, or the Ecclesiastical Courts. He was certainly no manufacturer, no merchant, no gentleman farmer. His name was unknown to the scientific and learned societies, and he had never been seen taking part in the deliberations of the Royal Institution, the London Institution, the Artisan’s Association, or the Institution of Arts and Sciences. He belonged, in short, to none of the countless societies that swarm in the English capital, from the Harmonic to that of the Entomologists, founded chiefly to abolish pernicious insects.

source_text: Passepartout was on the point of vigorously resenting the epithet, the reason of which he could not for the life of him comprehend; but he reflected that the unfortunate Fix was probably very much disappointed and humiliated in his self-esteem, after having so awkwardly followed a false scent around the world, and refrained.
modern_text: Passepartout was on the point of vigorously resenting the epithet, the reason for which he could not for the life of him understand; but he reflected that the unfortunate Fix was probably very much disappointed and humiliated in his self-esteem, after having so awkwardly followed a false trail around the world, and let it pass.
